flaw.ctx: You asked whether N more people can be seated with nobody new next to anyone.
flaw.answer: It never checks the **right** neighbour, so it seats someone directly beside an existing person: `[1,0,0,1]` gives 1 instead of 0, and the stated row admits 4. It also crashes on `null`.
flaw.fix: Require both neighbours free (treating the ends as free), and guard null.
flaw.verified: compiled against this problem's stage tests by npm run verify

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given:
> 
> [1,0,0,0,0,0,1,0,0]
> 
> Determine whether N additional people can be seated where no new person sits next to another person.
> 
> Expected:
> 
> 3 → true
> 4 → false
> 
> Also handle:
> 
> [1,0,0,1,0,0,1,0,0]
> 
> and:
> 
> [0]

A row of seats, some taken. Fit as many more people in as possible with nobody ever seated directly beside anybody, then compare against N.

A boolean, but compute the **maximum** first and compare. Returning the maximum is more useful, more testable, and no more work.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
Does the existing arrangement have to be valid? `[1,1,0]` has two people already adjacent. The question asks only about **new** people — "no new person sits next to another person" — so an already-invalid row is simply the starting state and is not rejected.

That reading is confirmed by the phrasing and it is worth stating, because the alternative (validate first, throw if invalid) changes the contract. My tests skip pre-invalid rows when cross-checking the two implementations, which is a deliberate choice about what is in scope rather than an oversight.

Second, minor: `N = 0` is trivially true, and negative N should be too. One line.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| The existing arrangement may already be invalid. | The question is only about new people. Validating first would be a different contract — state the reading. |
| Out-of-bounds neighbours count as free. | So position 0 has only a right neighbour. Getting this wrong makes `[0]` return 0 instead of 1, which is one of the supplied cases. |
| The input must not be mutated. | The greedy needs to mark seats as it goes, so it works on a clone. A caller whose array is silently modified by a query is a real bug, and the test asserts it does not happen. |
| `N <= 0` is true. | Trivially. One line, and it avoids an unnecessary scan. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Scan left to right and take every seat you legally can. That is the whole algorithm, and the question is **why it is optimal** — because "greedy works here" is the claim an interviewer will push on.

The exchange argument: suppose some optimal seating does *not* use the leftmost available seat `i`, and instead uses some seat `j > i`. Occupying `i` only constrains `i-1` and `i+1`. Since `i` was the leftmost available seat, `i-1` was not available anyway. So moving that person from `j` to `i` can only free up seats to the right, never block any — the count does not decrease. Repeat, and any optimal solution can be rewritten into the leftmost-first one without losing anybody. Therefore leftmost-first is optimal.

The mechanical point is that the scan must **see its own decisions**. Having seated someone at `i`, the check at `i+1` has to know that. Working on a clone and writing the seat back is the simplest way; carrying the index of the last occupied seat is the O(1)-space way. Either is fine; reading the original array while pretending it was updated is the bug.

And then the boundaries, which is where this is actually got wrong: **position 0 has no left neighbour and the last position has no right neighbour**, and both count as free. `[0]` returns 1 precisely because of that, which is presumably why it was supplied as a case.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Enumerate every subset of the free seats, check each for adjacency violations, and take the largest valid one. *O(2^n · n). O(n) space.*

**Why not good enough.** Exponential for a problem that is linear, and it also teaches nothing — it cannot answer "why is greedy right" because it never makes a choice. The useful intermediate thought is per-gap arithmetic: a run of `g` free seats bounded by occupied seats admits `(g-1)/2` people, and a run at the end of the array admits `g/2`. That closed form is correct and is a fine alternative answer, but it needs four cases depending on which ends are bounded, and the greedy scan handles all four without enumerating them.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | A 0/1 array and an integer N |
| TRANSFORMATION | None — the array is already the state |
| DATA STRUCTURE | None. A clone of the array, or a single integer for the last occupied index. |
| ALGORITHM | Left to right, seat at any free position whose neighbours are both free, counting out-of-bounds as free |
| OUTPUT | The maximum number of additional people, compared against N |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `N <= 0` → true.
- Clone the array.
- For each index `i` with `row[i] == 0`: check `i == 0 || row[i-1] == 0`, and `i == n-1 || row[i+1] == 0`.
- If both hold, set `row[i] = 1` and increment the count.
- Return whether the count is at least N.

- A new person needs both neighbours free. Out-of-bounds counts as free, which is where the bugs live.
- Existing people constrain but are not removed.
- One pass, O(1) extra space, is achievable.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| A clone rather than mutating the input | The scan must see its own decisions, and a query that modifies its argument is a bug waiting to happen. One allocation, and the test asserts the original is untouched. |
| Or a single `lastTaken` index for O(1) space | The only history the check needs is whether the immediately preceding seat is occupied, which one integer records. Initialised to -2 so index 0 correctly has no left neighbour. |
| Compute the maximum, then compare | More useful than a bare boolean, identical cost, and far easier to test — you can assert a number rather than probing a predicate. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`(int[])seats.Clone()`.** The scan writes `row[i] = 1` so that the check at `i+1` sees it. Doing that to the caller’s array would make a read-only-looking query destructive. The test asserts `row[2]` is still 0 afterwards, because this is exactly the kind of thing that passes review and surprises someone later.

**`i == 0 || row[i-1] == 0` — short-circuit as the boundary check.** The `||` is doing the out-of-bounds handling: at `i == 0` the left is treated as free without ever indexing `-1`. Same on the right with `i == row.Length - 1`. Writing it this way means there are no special cases and no separate first/last handling — which is why `[0]` works with no extra code.

**Why `row[i] = 1` and not just a counter.** The decision has to be visible to the next iteration. A version that counts without marking would seat people at both `i` and `i+1`, which is the single most common bug here and produces roughly double the correct answer on an empty row.

**`lastTaken = -2` in the constant-space version.** `leftFree` is `lastTaken < i - 1`. At `i = 0` that needs `lastTaken < -1`, so -1 would be wrong and -2 is the smallest value that works. An off-by-one in a sentinel, and the reason the two implementations are cross-checked on 4,000 random rows rather than trusted.

**Returning the maximum rather than the boolean.** `MaxAdditional` is the real function and `CanSeat` is a one-line wrapper. Every test asserts a number, which localises a failure to the exact row rather than to a yes/no.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MaxAdditional` | O(n) | O(n) | One pass; the clone is the space |
| `MaxAdditionalNoCopy` | O(n) | O(1) | One pass, one integer of history |
| `CanSeat` | O(n) | O(1) or O(n) | Delegates |

**There is an early-exit worth mentioning and not taking.** `CanSeat` could stop as soon as the count reaches N, which is faster on a true answer and identical on a false one. I return the maximum instead, because the maximum is the more useful value and the input is a row of seats — the constant factor is irrelevant. Saying you noticed and chose not to is better than either doing it silently or missing it.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `[0]` | 1. Both neighbours out of bounds. A supplied case, and the boundary test. |
| `[1]` | 0. |
| Empty array | 0, guarded first. |
| Null | 0. State the choice. |
| `N = 0` | True without scanning. |
| Negative N | True. |
| All free, length 5 | 3 — seats at 0, 2, 4. |
| `[1,0,1]` | 0 — a gap of one admits nobody. |
| `[1,0,0,1]` | 0 — a gap of two admits nobody. |
| `[1,0,0,0,1]` | 1 — a gap of three admits exactly one. |
| Already-invalid row `[1,1,0]` | Accepted as the starting state; only new placements are constrained. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Prove the greedy is optimal.**

Take any optimal seating that does not use the leftmost available seat `i`, and let `j > i` be the first seat it does use. Occupying `i` constrains only `i-1` and `i+1`, and `i-1` was already unavailable since `i` was leftmost. So moving that person from `j` to `i` keeps the seating valid and frees space to the right rather than blocking it. The count is unchanged, so the result is still optimal. Repeat until the seating is leftmost-first — therefore leftmost-first achieves the optimum.

*Trade-off:* None; it is a proof, not a choice. Being able to give it in three sentences is what separates "I remembered this is greedy" from "I know why".

**People need k empty seats between them, not 1.**

Seat at `i` if no occupied seat lies within distance `k` on either side. With the `lastTaken` formulation it is one comparison: `lastTaken < i - k`, plus a forward check that the next `k` seats hold nobody. Keeping a **next occupied index** alongside `lastTaken`, precomputed in one backward pass, makes the forward check O(1) and the whole thing still one pass.

*Trade-off:* Naively the forward check is O(k) per position, so O(nk) overall — fine for small k. The precomputed next-occupied array makes it O(n) at the cost of O(n) space. The exchange argument still holds, so the greedy is still optimal, which is the thing worth confirming rather than assuming.

**The row is circular — it is a round table.**

With no occupied seats, a circle of n admits `floor(n/2)`, which the linear greedy gets wrong on an all-empty row (it would seat both ends, which are adjacent on a circle). The standard fix is to case-split on the first position: run the linear algorithm once assuming seat 0 is used and once assuming it is not, and take the better. If any seat is already occupied, cut the circle there and the problem becomes linear with both ends bounded.

*Trade-off:* Two passes instead of one, still O(n). The real point is that the greedy’s optimality proof depended on the array having an end, so the circular case needs the argument redone rather than the code tweaked — which is exactly the same lesson as the obstacle follow-up in Q3.

**Return the seat positions, not just the count.**

Collect `i` into a list when seating. Note that the positions are not unique: for `[0,0,0]` both `{0,2}` and, with a different greedy, other pairs of size 1 exist — so the count is unique and the arrangement is not. Say which one you return (leftmost-first).

*Trade-off:* O(k) extra space for k seats. The only subtlety is stating that ties exist, which matters if a caller is going to compare against an expected arrangement rather than an expected count.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Null? n = 0? A row already invalid (two adjacent people)?* — Null → only n = 0 fits; n = 0 is always true; ask about invalid rows

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Why is greedy optimal?* — Seating at the leftmost possible seat never blocks more than a later choice
